rv.q: Beginning in pain and provocation, it finds its way to splendor.
Dev, like Prince Faggot itself, may be more in awe of the throne than he would prefer to admit.

What emerges from all this is a play that is as self-conscious as it is self-revealing, a work that does not merely portray queer desire but actively excavates its sedimented histories, its inherited traumas, its ideological entanglements.
In other words, “Prince Faggot” is meta-theater at its best and most thought-provoking.
It is erotic and stunningly beautiful.
“Prince Faggot,” wonderfully acted and artfully staged, turns out to be surprisingly earnest, thoughtful, even respectful.
Tannahill nonetheless vividly interrogates the paradox of identity and identification.
I struggle to reconcile how the play’s two strands communicate with each other.
It's also a telling symptom of a play that doesn't always know where its real strengths lie.
An uneven drama, Prince Faggot proves scarcely as meaningful about present and future queer existence as its author intends, although it can be surprisingly entertaining in spots.
Jordan Tannahill‘s play is a dense tapestry of wonder, imagination, sexuality, humor and stinging observation.
Prince Faggot is theater that shocks in the best way: not for outrage, but for revelation. It's radical, raw, and alive.
Tannahill crafts his scenes with care, and even some of the most outrageous moments are grounded in a kind of hyper-reality.
Can a play provocatively titled Prince Faggot actually be a philosophical meditation of queer identity? In this case, yes.
Under Shayok Misha Chowdhury’s careful direction, the action moves forward seamlessly and understandably.

Both descriptions can be applied to Prince Faggot, which feels like two separate plays that don’t quite merge; one is more realistic, and far more engaging; the other irreverent, and far less cohesive.

cn.t: Tannahill's provocatively titled play explodes with entertainment value, blending personal queer histories with speculative royal fiction. Critics find it bold and engaging, though some question whether its taboo-treading premise fully delivers.
